<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-structured cases and handled the pressure round with proper A1/A2 formatting, making this a genuinely close debate. But CON's "value capture" frame (bans give away upzoning value for free; bonuses price it and extract affordability/siting commitments) proved more resilient under fire. When PRO argued that discretionary friction inflates costs into luxury infill, CON's reply that "delay is trivial next to land costs, and what removes friction raises what speculators will pay for the lot" directly punctured that mechanism, and PRO never returned to repair it in Rebuttal 2 or Closing, instead pivoting to filtering effects and a "your guarantee isn't perfect either" tu quoque. Similarly, CON's reframe that spreading upzoning "universalizes" rather than "dilutes" speculative pressure on starter homes, and its dilemma on the zoning/permitting distinction ("either the veto still exists for safety, or it's gone and overload is legalized"), landed cleanly and went largely unrebutted in substance. PRO's real strengths — Minneapolis/Auckland grounding and the "fight once vs. fight forever" political-durability argument — kept the debate competitive and were not fully answered by CON, but PRO's case relied more on reasserting supply-side optimism than dismantling CON's central logic. PRO's opening was also clipped for exceeding the word limit, a real execution cost per the judging rules. On balance CON's rebuttals did more damage to PRO's live mechanisms than the reverse, and CON's closing framing ("who gets paid for the upzone") gave the clearer decision rule.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 1 point that "delay is trivial next to land and construction costs... lower friction does not lower rent, it raises what a speculator will pay for the lot" directly neutralized PRO's core "friction causes luxury infill" mechanism, and PRO never circled back to repair it in later speeches.</best_rebuttal>
